title: The scholar of Konya
hookLine: he becomes a respected teacher of Islamic law and theology in Konya, Anatolia

cards: Some people grow up into their parent's job. The kid who took over the family store, the doctor whose mother was a doctor, the pastor's son who became the pastor. People nod at them in the street.
They're solid. They're safe. Konya, the early 1240s.
A man in his mid-thirties, in a scholar's robe and a large turban, walks to teach his classes with students trailing behind him. People bring him legal questions and wait for his answer.
He is exactly what everyone expected. If his life had stopped here, he might be remembered only as a learned man of Konya.

teach.b: Konya in the 1200s was the capital of the Seljuk sultans of Rum, a Muslim kingdom in Anatolia, full of mosques, schools and caravans. The sources say the sultan invited Rumi's father to teach there.
In 1231 the father died, and his post passed to his son, who was about twenty-four. That's young to inherit a pulpit, so the son kept studying.
Burhan al-Din of Tirmidh, a former student of his father, came to Konya and, the accounts say, trained him for about nine years, in books and in the inner life of prayer and fasting.
The young man also studied in Aleppo and Damascus, two old centers of learning.

teach.h: A TEACHER OF LAW AND THEOLOGY.
teach.b: By the early 1240s he was a respected teacher of Islamic law and theology, what Muslims call fiqh and kalam. He taught in a school, preached in the mosque, gave legal opinions, and was addressed as Mowlana, our master.
He had a wife and sons; the oldest, Sultan Walad, would one day write his father's story. Here's what's worth noticing. The sources show no sign yet of the poet.
They describe a learned, careful, deeply religious man. The wildness came later, and it grew out of this ground, not against it.
His poems are full of the Qur'an and of law and theology, because he'd spent his whole life inside them.
The respectable one was not a mask he later threw off. It was the soil.

how: Readers of Rumi often begin with his life as a scholar: he taught Islamic law and theology in Konya, and biographies stress that his later poetry grew out of that learning.

games.q: you're twenty-four. your father, a well-known teacher, has just died, and his students look at you. what do you do?
o: take his place, and keep studying for years.
leave Konya and start fresh somewhere else.
refuse the post until you feel ready.
games.why: he took the post and kept learning: nine years with Burhan al-Din, study in Aleppo and Damascus. the young heir became a real scholar.

practice: If the people who know you described you in three words, what would they say? Reliable, funny, the one who fixes things, the one who's always busy.
Say the words inside, then ask gently: is that all of me, or is there something in me nobody has met yet? Don't answer quickly; leave the question open.

wordCard.voice: Mowlana, our master: the title Rumi's students used for him as a teacher of Islamic law and theology. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian and Arabic: our master. the title his students used, and the name many still use for him.

carryVoice: Your line: the respectable one. It can be true without being the whole story. Day one hundred fifty-nine, in the books.
